fatal_errors: The cited evidence concerns spray-coated nanoflakes tested only in an ambient steel-on-steel contact; it provides no support for performance on CoCrFeNi or at temperatures approaching 800 °C.

The central prediction of low, nearly temperature-invariant friction and wear through 800 °C is unsupported and conflicts with the acknowledged possibility of coating oxidation or delamination at high temperature.

The proposed mechanism claims suppression of deleterious oxidation but does not establish a high-temperature lubricating oxide or molybdate pathway comparable to the mechanism required across 600–800 °C.
Loads, contact geometry, sliding speed, distance, counterface, coating thickness, and environmental composition are not fixed, so the claimed operating envelope is not quantitatively defined.
explanation: The response addresses the general wide-temperature lubrication problem and proposes a clear single intervention with a controlled coated-versus-uncoated experiment. It is also a novel alternative rather than a reconstruction of the target, which varied Mo content in an SPS-fabricated CoCrFeNiMox–Ni/MoS2–Ag–Cr2O3 composite. It misses the target material state, Mo-induced lattice distortion and sigma-phase strengthening, low-temperature MoS2/Ag lubrication, and high-temperature silver-molybdate glaze formation. More importantly, its evidence supports excellent room-temperature performance only for a steel tribopair. Extrapolating that result to CoCrFeNi under dry sliding from room temperature to 800 °C is not evidence-disciplined, especially because sulfide-containing nanoflakes may oxidize or delaminate. The falsification design is directionally sound, but it needs fixed loads and tribological parameters plus explicit numerical success thresholds to distinguish the hypothesis robustly.
